title: Redwood Discovery - Cascade AI - Latency & Throughput
summary: Discovery focused on p95 latency targets for streaming and non-streaming use cases, concurrency needs (~200-1k), token/sec benchmarking, and tradeoffs between Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Customer is evaluating for a conversational agent with multimodal extensions and strict data residency requirements.
action_items: Emma Nguyen: Share latency benchmark spreadsheet and Redwood hosted vs dedicated pricing (due 2026-07-20)
Carlos Ruiz: Schedule 2-hour technical deep-dive POC scoping with Omar and Maya (due 2026-07-22)
Leah Park: Provide representative prompt set and peak concurrency schedule (due 2026-07-18)
next_steps: Redwood to send benchmark template and pricing sheet
Schedule POC scoping session (2 hours) to nail down hardware targets and dataset for token/sec runs
Customer to share security questionnaire; Redwood to return SOC2/KMS docs
transcript:
[2026-07-15 14:30:02] Meeting started
Header: 2026-07-15 14:30 PDT | Duration: 56m | Attendees: Emma (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood SE) - Leah (Cascade CTO), Omar (Lead ML Eng), Maya (SRE), Jon (Eng Mgr)

Summary (auto): Quick intros, high-level product fit, deep dive on latency/throughput targets, questions about dedicated/private deployment and security. Ended with next steps and POC scoping.

[00:00:12] Emma Nguyen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I am Emma with Redwood, i'm the account lead, um to my left is Carlos and Priya who will jump into the technicals — maybe quick intros from your side?
[00:00:22] Leah Park: Yep hi i'm Leah Park CTO at Cascade AI, we build a customer-facing conversational agent for financial planning, um curious about latency — our SLAs target p95 under 300ms for short responses and p95 under 1s for longer streaming flows.
[00:00:38] Omar Singh: Hey i'm Omar, we handle model infra and want to understand token/sec benchmarks and how concurrency affects p95 and tail latencies, also curious about your hosted vs dedicated cost tradeoffs.
[00:00:50] Carlos Ruiz: Great, thanks. Quick note: Redwood supports hosted, dedicated reserved capacity, and private VPC/on-prem — with consistent API. We typically benchmark both non-streaming and streaming paths, and measure p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec under specified concurrency.
[00:01:05] Maya Patel: We have regulatory requirements so VPC and KMS integration matter. Also audit logs retention.
[00:01:13] Priya Shah: Totally, we can cover that. Can I ask about typical prompt lengths and concurrency?
[00:01:21] Leah Park: Typical prompt is 60-120 tokens, response 20-150 tokens depending on context, and peak concurrency tends to be 600-900 active sessions during market open, baseline ~200. We do streaming for progressive responses.

[00:02:05] Carlos Ruiz: Ok that's helpful. For streaming use cases we look at token emit latency and chunking behavior; p95 end-to-end for first token and subsequent tokens differs. In hosted we usually hit ~80-200 tokens/sec per GPU for certain open models in 8-bit quantized paths with our optimizations, but it depends on model and seq length. For dedicated we can guarantee throughput with reserved GPU pools.
[00:02:40] Omar Singh: When you say 80-200 tokens/sec per GPU — which model / quantization are we talking about? Our experiments used Llama 3 70B quantized to 4-bit and saw around 120 tokens/sec on A100-ish hardware.
[00:02:56] Carlos Ruiz: Right, so numbers vary. Our benchmark spreadsheet shows Mistral/Redwood-verified variants and LLama-family numbers. For 70B-4bit on A100, you might see 100-150 tokens/sec depending on batching and KV cache reuse. On H100 and optimized kernels it's higher. We can run a targeted token/sec run during a POC on your payloads.

[00:03:30] Emma Nguyen: Two quick qualification things — timeline and success criteria?
[00:03:35] Leah Park: Timeline is Q4 pilot -> Q1 rollout. Success criteria: p95 < 350ms for short non-stream responses, p95 < 1s for streaming first-token (and steady-state token latency < 60ms), and predictable cost per 1M tokens. Also auditability and encryption keys for customer data.

[00:04:05] Jon Rivera: And we need autoscaling behavior for spikes up to 1k concurrent requests without dropping sessions.

[00:04:20] Carlos Ruiz: Ok good. On autoscaling, Dedicated offers reserved pools with configurable autoscale and burst; we can set min pool to handle baseline and burst handles spikes. Hosted has soft limits and we route by policy — but for strict SLAs dedicated or private is usually required.

[00:04:50] Omar Singh: If we go dedicated, how does routing work across AZs/regions? We want failover and geo routing.
[00:04:58] Priya Shah: We support multi-region deployment and smart routing by policy. We also provide automatic fallback to smaller model variants if capacity constrained, which helps maintain availability under load.

[00:05:20] Leah Park: Can you talk about latency profiling — how do you measure p95? Is it end-to-end from our client to response, or internal server-side?
[00:05:29] Carlos Ruiz: We measure both. In dashboards we show token-level timing, network time, and end-to-end. For p95 guarantees we typically mean server-side processing time; network will add variance depending on customer setup, but we can instrument and provide traces.

[00:05:55] Emma Nguyen: We have a benchmark template we'll share — it captures prompt distribution, concurrency schedule, desired p95 targets, and allowed model variants. We'll pre-run on hosted/dev clusters and then run a POC on dedicated if you want.

[00:06:12] Omar Singh: On the POC runs, are they reproducible? We need deterministic batching and warm KV cache to mimic user sessions.
[00:06:20] Carlos Ruiz: Yes, we can simulate sessions with KV cache warmup and prefix caching. We can run steady-state and cold-start scenarios; we'll include both in the template. Also quantization profile matters — we'll test your chosen model with float16, int8, and available 4-bit paths to show accuracy vs tokens/sec tradeoffs.

[00:07:00] Maya Patel: Security questions — do you support customer-managed KMS and do you provide audit logs at token-level?
[00:07:07] Priya Shah: Yes to KMS for Private and Dedicated. Hosted supports envelope encryption with customer KMS for enterprise tiers. Audit logs are available; retention depends on plan but we have options for longer retention as an add-on.

[00:07:25] Omar Singh: Any gotchas around streaming and reorder/dropped chunks? We care about stable progressive tokens.
[00:07:33] Carlos Ruiz: We stream in chunks and have mechanisms for ensuring order; network retries can cause duplication — we surface chunk IDs and sequence numbers so you can dedupe. For ultra-low-latency streaming we recommend smaller chunk sizes and a dedicated endpoint to reduce queuing.

[00:08:05] Leah Park: For throughput cost modeling — what's the unit economics when moving from hosted to dedicated?
[00:08:13] Emma Nguyen: Hosted is usage-based; dedicated is capacity-based with reserve commitments. For high sustained concurrency dedicated usually reduces per-token cost. We'll send a pricing comparison sheet with example workload math.

[00:08:35] Omar Singh: We run scheduled overnight batch generation as well — any recommendations on batching vs streaming for cost?
[00:08:42] Carlos Ruiz: Batch generation for non-interactive flows is ideal — you can increase sequence parallelism and reduce per-token cost. For interactive flows, streaming is better for perceived latency but can raise per-token cost if you don't enable caching. Redwood Optimize suggests batching windows and caching configuration per route.

[00:09:10] Jon Rivera: About concurrency: we expect 600-900 during peak, but sessions have state. How do you handle long-lived KV caches memory usage?
[00:09:20] Carlos Ruiz: We manage KV cache per session with configurable eviction policies. For large numbers of long-lived sessions we recommend dedicated pools sized to hold warm caches, or prefix caching on a caching tier. We can provide memory vs throughput tradeoffs in the POC.

[00:09:45] Leah Park: Could you run us through an example p95 benchmark output?
[00:09:50] Carlos Ruiz: Sure — (screen share note) typical benchmark CSV: columns for model, quant, seq_in, seq_out, concurrency, tokens/sec, p50_ms, p95_ms, p99_ms, error_rate. Example: Llama3-70B-4bit, 80/40, concurrency 200, tokens/sec 130, p50 40ms, p95 260ms, p99 420ms. For streaming first-token might be p95 700-900ms for heavier prompts on hosted; on dedicated we can bring that down.

[00:10:40] Omar Singh: Those numbers look reasonable. For our 1s p95 streaming first-token target, do you think dedicated on H100s is required?
[00:10:48] Carlos Ruiz: Likely yes for consistent tail latency at high concurrency. But we can explore mixed routing: critical users to dedicated, less-critical to hosted.

[00:11:05] Maya Patel: SLA and compliance — what's the typical SLA for dedicated?
[00:11:10] Priya Shah: We offer SLA-backed uptime and latency targets for Dedicated with monitoring and runbooks. Exact numbers depend on contract tier; enterprise packages include higher uptime, faster incident response, and dedicated support.

[00:11:28] Leah Park: Any pitfalls around model variants when falling back? We worry about hallucination/regression when switching models.

[00:11:35] Carlos Ruiz: Good point; we suggest model-matching policies where variance is minimized — e.g., fall back to a quantized variant of the same family and we run evals on your prompt set to measure regression. Redwood Optimize flags quality regressions tied to prompt sets.

[00:12:05] Emma Nguyen: Ok, operationally for a POC we propose: 1) client shares prompt set and concurrency profile, 2) Redwood runs hosted baseline benchmarks, 3) optional dedicated scoped run with target hardware, 4) follow-up deep-dive on results. Does that align?
[00:12:21] Leah Park: Yes that sounds good. Timeline — can you turn the initial benchmark in three business days?
[00:12:27] Emma Nguyen: We'll try for 3-5 business days once we have the prompt set. Carlos will pick a slot for the dedicated scoping.

[00:12:40] Omar Singh: I'm also curious about instrumentation — can you expose token-level traces to our SREs?
[00:12:46] Priya Shah: We expose per-request traces and token timing in our console and via tracing hooks. For Private deployments you can ship traces to your own observability stack.

[00:13:05] Jon Rivera: What about cold-start behavior — for sessions with no warm cache, how bad is the p95?
[00:13:12] Carlos Ruiz: Cold-start can add 100-300ms depending on model size and KV init. We measure cold vs warm and include both in reports. Warm sessions with prefix caching perform much better.

[00:13:40] Leah Park: Any recommendations for chunk size and buffer duration for streaming to balance latency vs throughput?
[00:13:48] Carlos Ruiz: Smaller chunks (8-16 tokens) reduce first-byte latency but increase overhead. Larger chunks increase throughput. Buffer duration of ~50-150ms is common; Redwood Optimize can suggest per-route defaults.

[00:14:10] Omar Singh: For the dedicated pool, how quickly can we scale up in a burst? Say sudden spike to 1k conc — do you have warm spare capacity?
[00:14:20] Priya Shah: You can configure burst capacity; dedicated contracts allow burst buffers or autoscale policies with pre-warmed nodes. For strict requirements we recommend reserved headroom.

[00:14:40] Emma Nguyen: Shall we talk about data residency and private deployment options?
[00:14:45] Leah Park: Yes — we need EU data residency for EU customers and SOC2 type II, with keys in our KMS.

[00:14:53] Priya Shah: We offer Private deployments with customer-managed networking and KMS, and will provide SOC2 artifacts. For EU residency we can deploy in region or provide on-prem if needed.

[00:15:10] Omar Singh: Is telemetry removed for private? We can't allow logs to cross tenants.

[00:15:15] Carlos Ruiz: In Private, the control plane can be customer-managed and logs stay in your environment. We support strict isolation.

[00:15:30] Leah Park: Ok good. Back to benchmarks — will you also measure token generation variance across repeated runs?
[00:15:36] Carlos Ruiz: Yes we run repeated trials to capture variance and p99 tails; we include error rates and CPU/GPU metrics.

[00:16:00] Emma Nguyen: Let's capture next steps: we'll send the benchmark template, pricing, and security docs. We will schedule the 2-hour POC scoping with Carlos.

[00:16:12] Jon Rivera: Can we get a list of recommended models and quantization settings for our use case?
[00:16:17] Priya Shah: We'll include our recommendations based on your prompt sizes and latency targets.

[00:16:30] Leah Park: Perfect. A couple quick follow-ups — do you have any references of similar customers with low-latency streaming?
[00:16:36] Emma Nguyen: We can share anonymized case studies and a contact with permission.

[00:16:45] Omar Singh: For the POC, what telemetry do you need from us? Prompt set, concurrency schedule, example logs, maybe network topology.

[00:16:54] Carlos Ruiz: Exactly that — plus desired model candidates.

[00:17:12] Maya Patel: Are there any limits around API rate limiting and token bucket behavior? We need predictable throttling.
[00:17:18] Priya Shah: We expose rate limiting and quotas per route and you can configure burst tokens. For Dedicated you can bump limits.

[00:17:35] Emma Nguyen: Anything else before we wrap?
[00:17:38] Leah Park: Not from me. Thanks — this was helpful.

[00:17:45] Emma Nguyen: Great thanks everyone — we'll send the template and schedule the POC scoping.

[00:17:52] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings: "KV cache" heard as "K V cash" in one spot, "Llama" sometimes transcribed as "Lama". Speakers overlapped briefly at 00:12 when scheduling.
